title: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism after Total Hip or Knee Replacement
abstract: BACKGROUND: Studies comparing aspirin with anticoagulants for venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty have had conflicting results. METHODS: In a comparative-effectiveness noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned patients undergoing elective hip or knee arthroplasty to receive aspirin (81 mg twice daily), warfarin (to a target international normalized ratio of 2.0), or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) for 30 days. The composite primary effectiveness outcome (death from any cause or symptomatic VTE) and primary safety outcome (bleeding, reoperation for wound problems, or myocardial infarction) were evaluated through 6 months in a blinded fashion. The noninferiority margin for the risk difference was 0.69 percentage points. RESULTS: Among 18,883 participants who had undergone randomization, 15,317 (7214 with hip arthroplasty and 8103 with knee arthroplasty) were included in the primary per-protocol analysis. A primary effectiveness outcome event occurred in 77 of 6090 participants (1.26%) in the aspirin group, in 52 of 4231 (1.23%) in the warfarin group, and in 47 of 4996 (0.94%) in the rivaroxaban group; a primary safety outcome event occurred in 177 (2.91%), 142 (3.36%), and 174 (3.48%), respectively. In pairwise comparisons, 6-month risks of a primary effectiveness outcome event were 1.24% and 0.94% for aspirin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.30 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.20 to 0.81); 1.24% and 1.01% for aspirin versus warfarin (difference, 0.23 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.34 to 0.81); and 1.13% and 1.10% for warfarin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.03 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.57 to 0.63). Risks of a primary safety outcome event were 3.70% and 3.02% for rivaroxaban versus aspirin (difference, 0.68 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.41); 3.65% and 2.88% for warfarin versus aspirin (difference, 0.77 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.58); and 3.59% and 3.61% for rivaroxaban versus warfarin (difference, -0.02 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.89 to 0.85). Intention-to-treat analyses yielded similar results. CONCLUSIONS: Aspirin prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty was not noninferior to rivaroxaban or warfarin with respect to death or symptomatic VTE. Warfarin and rivaroxaban were not noninferior to aspirin for safety. (Funded by the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute; PEPPER ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02810704.).

title: Effect of discontinuing antihypertensives on perioperative hypotension in older patients before non-cardiac surgery: multicentre, randomised, double blind, controlled trial
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine whether discontinuing versus continuing angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) on the morning of surgery reduces perioperative hypotension in older patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery. DESIGN: Multicentre, randomised, double blind, placebo controlled trial. SETTING: Five tertiary teaching hospitals in China, November 2020 to December 2023. PARTICIPANTS: 2036 older patients (60-80 years) using ACE inhibitors or ARBs for at least two weeks and scheduled for non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomised to receive their usual ACE inhibitor or ARB or a placebo in identical capsules on the morning of surgery. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome was the incidence of perioperative hypotension (mean blood pressure <65 mm Hg or a ≥30% decrease from baseline requiring treatment). Secondary outcomes included duration of hypotension, requirement for a vasopressor, intraoperative fluid volume, postoperative hypotension, and 30 day complications (neurocognitive disorders, major cardiocerebral events) or mortality. RESULTS: 2012 patients (mean age 68.8 years; 54.4% male) completed the study: 1004 were included in the antihypertensive group and 1008 in the no antihypertensive group. The incidence of perioperative hypotension was lower in the no antihypertensive group (314/1008, 31.2%) versus antihypertensive group (457/1004, 45.5%): adjusted odds ratio 0.52 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.43 to 0.63); absolute risk difference -14.4% (95% CI -18.5% to -10.1%); P<0.001. The duration of hypotension and requirement for a vasopressor were both reduced in the no antihypertensive group: adjusted mean difference -1.3 minutes (95% CI -1.8 to -0.8 minutes) and 28.5% v 41.1%; adjusted odds ratio 0.54 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.66). Intraoperative fluid volume, postoperative hypotension, 30 day complications, and mortality did not differ significantly between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Discontinuing ACE inhibitors or ARBs on the morning of surgery in older patients with hypertension statistically significantly reduced perioperative hypotension and the requirement for vasopressors without increasing 30 day complications or mortality. This simple strategy provides high certainty evidence for preoperative drug management in this patient population. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2000039376.

title: Effect of intensive blood pressure control on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes: prespecified analysis of secondary outcomes of BPROAD randomised controlled trial
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effect of intensive compared with standard treatment of systolic blood pressure (SBP) on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes. DESIGN: Multicentre, open label, outcome assessor masked, randomised controlled trial. SETTING: 145 clinical centres across seven geographical regions in China. PARTICIPANTS: 12 821 adults aged ≥50 years with type 2 diabetes, raised SBP, and increased cardiovascular risk, of whom 12 434 without probable dementia at baseline were included in this cognitive ancillary study. Further assessments were performed annually and at the end of study. INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomly assigned to receive intensive treatment targeting SBP <120 mm Hg or standard treatment targeting SBP <140 mm Hg for up to five years. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary cognitive outcome was a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Secondary cognitive outcomes included all cause dementia, mild cognitive impairment, changes in cognitive functions, and changes in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics. A subset of participants underwent brain MRI at baseline (n=862) and at the end of study (n=605) to assess changes in white matter lesion volume and total brain volume. RESULTS: 6219 participants were assigned to receive intensive treatment and 6215 to receive standard treatment. Baseline mean age was 63.7 years, and 5567 (44.8%) participants were women. After one year, mean SBP was 121.6 mm Hg in the intensive treatment group and 133.2 mm Hg in the standard treatment group. During a median follow-up of 3.8 years, the primary cognitive outcome of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment occurred in 747 participants (3.69 events per 100 person years) in the intensive treatment group and 783 participants (3.89 events per 100 person years) in the standard treatment group (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 1.06; P=0.38). In the MRI substudy (428 intensive treatment v 434 standard treatment), the intensive treatment group had a smaller increase in white matter lesion volume compared with the standard treatment group (between group difference -0.09 inverse hyperbolic sine (asinh) transformed cm3, 95% CI -0.15 to -0.02; P=0.01). CONCLUSIONS: Over a median of about four years, no statistically significant difference in incidence of a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment was observed among adults with type 2 diabetes receiving standard treatment of SBP (target <140 mm Hg) and intensive treatment (target <120 mm Hg). Intensive treatment was, however, associated with a reduction in the accrual of cerebral white matter lesion volume. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03808311.

title: Alcohol and cardiovascular disease: inter-organ crosstalk, microvascular dysfunction, and cardiovascular ageing
abstract: Alcohol-related cardiovascular risk is being fundamentally reappraised. Observational associations suggesting cardioprotection with light-to-moderate drinking have been challenged by contemporary cohort analyses, Mendelian-randomization studies, biomarker-informed investigations, and updated public-health guidance. Uncertainty nevertheless persists at very low exposure levels and for selected coronary or all-cause outcomes. Alcohol is therefore best viewed as a dose-, pattern-, and host-dependent cardiovascular stressor. Acute or binge drinking, sustained heavy intake, chronic intake with episodic binges, and withdrawal produce overlapping but distinct phenotypes, including hypertension, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias, sudden death, alcohol-associated cardiomyopathy, heart failure, stroke, and vascular disease. A systems-cardiology framework is presented in which direct myocardial injury, electrical instability, haemodynamic and autonomic stress, vascular and microvascular dysfunction, and disrupted inter-organ signalling interact. Ethanol and acetaldehyde toxicity, redox imbalance, microbial and inflammatory mediators, neurohumoral activation, and metabolic or electrolyte disturbances can impair endothelial signalling, mitochondrial energetics, excitation-contraction coupling, electrical stability, and repair. Pathway dominance varies across exposure patterns and susceptible hosts; coronary microvascular dysfunction may represent a convergence pathway rather than an obligatory mediator. Cumulative injury can diminish perfusion, contractile, electrical, autonomic, and exercise reserve. Alcohol-related cardiovascular ageing is proposed as a unifying cumulative phenotype encompassing mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative and nitrative stress, inflammageing, senescence, impaired repair, circadian and epigenetic dysregulation, fibrosis, and ventriculo-arterial uncoupling, although direct human evidence remains incomplete. Age, biological sex, genetics, comorbidities, sleep-circadian disruption, nutrition, medications, and polysubstance misuse may modify pathway dominance and reversibility. Structured exposure assessment and alcohol reduction or abstinence, when indicated, are actionable components of cardiovascular prevention and care.

title: Cardiovascular Health Promotion for US Veterans: Current State, Gaps, and Strategies: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association
abstract: US veterans represent a large and diverse population with distinctive demographic characteristics, comorbidity profiles, and social determinants of health shaped by military service. These factors contribute to a high burden of cardiovascular risk and low attainment of ideal cardiovascular health. At the same time, the Department of Veterans Affairs, which operates the nation's largest integrated healthcare system, provides a unique infrastructure for delivering population-level cardiovascular disease prevention for veterans. Understanding its successes and ongoing challenges can inform broader strategies across all health systems for promoting health among veterans. This scientific statement applies the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 framework, expanded to include mental health and substance use, to evaluate veteran cardiovascular health. For each domain, we review guideline recommendations, barriers to achieving optimal health, and major Veterans Affairs programs such as Patient Aligned Care Teams, the MOVE! Weight Management Program for Veterans, Whole Health, telehealth-based interventions, and integrated mental health and substance use disorder services. Across domains, veterans receiving Veterans Affairs care often achieve outcomes that are equal to or better than those of their non-Veterans Affairs counterparts, reflecting the strengths of the system in coordinated, team-based care and research-driven implementation. Despite substantial progress, opportunities remain to improve veteran lifestyle behaviors, metabolic health, lipid and blood pressure control, engagement in mental health and substance use care, and detection and management of sleep disorders. Addressing these challenges at the Veterans Affairs will require continuing to expand care access, enhancing digital data integration, tailoring interventions to high-risk subgroups, and strengthening implementation strategies to improve uptake and engagement across Veterans Affairs services.

title: Cardiovascular outcomes with survodutide in adults with obesity at increased cardiovascular risk (SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Survodutide, a glucagon receptor and GLP-1 receptor dual agonist, improved markers of cardiometabolic health in people with obesity, but cardiovascular safety for this new class remains to be established. METHODS: SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT was a global, phase 3, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled, multicentre, event-driven, cardiovascular safety trial conducted at 524 clinical sites in 34 countries. We included participants aged 18 years or older with a BMI of 27 kg/m2 or greater and established cardiovascular disease or at least two obesity complications or risk factors for cardiovascular disease; participants with chronic kidney disease were eligible if they also had a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or greater. Participants were randomly assigned by interactive response technology (1:1:1) to once-weekly subcutaneous survodutide (up-titrated to 3·6 mg or 6·0 mg) or placebo. The primary endpoint was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, non-fatal stroke, non-fatal myocardial infarction, ischaemia-related coronary revascularisation, or heart failure event (targeting 189 primary endpoint events). We assessed the non-inferiority of pooled survodutide compared with placebo with a margin of 1·65 for the upper limit of the two-sided 95% CI of the hazard ratio (HR). Efficacy and safety analyses included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of survodutide or placebo. The primary analysis was performed according to the treatment-regimen estimand, which assessed treatment effects regardless of any early discontinuation of survodutide or placebo, temporary stop, the use of protocol-prohibited obesity medications, or a prolonged dose-escalation period. This completed trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06077864. FINDINGS: From Nov 20, 2023, to Nov 8, 2024, we screened 7753 participants, of whom 5530 (71·3%) participants were recruited and randomly assigned to treatment. 23 (0·4%) participants were not treated; 1836 (33·3%) of 5507 participants received survodutide 3·6 mg, 1835 (33·3%) received 6·0 mg, and 1836 (33·3%) received placebo; 2194 (39·8%) were female, 3313 (60·2%) were male, and 4332 (78·7%) were White. Median time in study was 22·0 months (IQR 20·1-23·7). 1029 (56·0%) in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 1039 (56·6%) in the survodutide 6·0 mg group, and 1083 (59·0%) in the placebo group remained on treatment until study closeout. The primary endpoint occurred in 136 (3·7%) of 3671 participants in the survodutide group and in 76 (4·1%) 1836 participants in the placebo group (HR 0·89 [95% CI 0·67-1·18; p<0·0001 for non-inferiority). Adverse events occurred in 1708 (93·0%) of 1836 participants with survodutide 3·6 mg, 1708 (93·1%) of 1835 with survodutide 6·0 mg, and 1571 (85·6%) of 1836 with placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with survodutide than in the placebo group (nausea occurred in 882 [48·0%] of 1836 participants in the 3·6 mg group and 900 [49·0%] of 1835 in the 6·0 mg group vs 223 [12·1%] of 1836 in the placebo group, and vomiting occurred in 582 [31·7%] participants in the 3·6 mg group and 623 [34·0%] in the 6·0 mg group vs 89 [4·8%] in the placebo group). Gastrointestinal adverse events leading to treatment discontinuations occurred in 354 (19·3%) participants in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 381 (20·8%) in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and 34 (1·9%) in the placebo group. Serious adverse events occurred at similar rates across treatment groups (413 [22·5%] in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 381 [20·8%] in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and 439 [23·9%] in the placebo group). Fatal adverse events were similar across treatment groups (16 [0·9%] in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 16 [0·9%] in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and 11 [0·6%] in the placebo group) and were primarily due to cardiac disorders (six [0·3%] in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, seven [0·4%] in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and six [0·3%] in the placebo group). INTERPRETATION: In participants with obesity with established cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease or at increased risk of cardiovascular disease, survodutide was not associated with increased risk for the primary composite endpoint of death from cardiovascular causes, non-fatal stroke, non-fatal myocardial infarction, ischaemia-related coronary revascularisation, or heart failure event compared with placebo. This cardiovascular safety trial provides clinicians with reassuring data that treatment with survodutide, a novel glucagon receptor-GLP-1 receptor dual agonist, is not associated with increased cardiovascular risk. FUNDING: Boehringer Ingelheim.

title: Tirzepatide in Adolescents With Obesity: The SURMOUNT-ADOLESCENTS Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract: IMPORTANCE: Information on the effects of tirzepatide, a once-weekly glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist approved for obesity management in adults with obesity, remains limited in adolescents. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of once-weekly tirzepatide in adolescents with obesity or overweight with at least 1 obesity-related complication. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This phase 3, randomized, double-blind, 72-week clinical trial was conducted at 31 medical research centers and hospitals in Canada, the Czech Republic, Israel, Italy, Poland, and the US from October 16, 2023, to June 2, 2026, among adolescents aged 12 years to younger than 18 years with obesity or overweight with at least 1 obesity-related complication. INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomized 2:1 to receive once-weekly subcutaneous tirzepatide, escalated to a maximum tolerated dose (5, 10, or 15 mg), or placebo for 72 weeks, in addition to healthy lifestyle intervention. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary end point was percent change in body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) from baseline to week 72. Key secondary end points included percentages of participants achieving BMI reductions of at least 5%, at least 10%, at least 15%, and at least 20%; changes in BMI SD score; BMI expressed as a percentage of the 95th percentile; and body weight, waist circumference, and physical functioning from baseline to week 72. Safety outcomes included treatment-emergent adverse events, serious adverse events, and discontinuations due to adverse events. RESULTS: A total of 160 participants were randomized to receive tirzepatide (n = 109) or placebo (n = 51). Mean (SD) age at baseline was 14.6 (1.6) years, 99 participants (61.9%) were female, mean body weight was 109.7 kg, and mean BMI was 38.6. At week 72, tirzepatide was associated with 18.5% reduction in BMI, compared with 0.5% increase in BMI with placebo, demonstrating superiority over placebo (estimated treatment difference, -19.0 [95% CI, -23.9 to -14.1] percentage points; P < .001). Of 10 key secondary outcomes, all demonstrated statistically significant differences favoring tirzepatide compared with placebo. Overall, 79.6% of tirzepatide-treated participants achieved BMI reduction of at least 5% compared with 28.5% of participants in the placebo group (risk difference, 51.2 [95% CI, 36.3-66.1] percentage points; P < .001). The most common adverse events with tirzepatide treatment were gastrointestinal (mostly mild to moderate). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In adolescents with obesity or overweight with obesity-related complications, tirzepatide, in addition to healthy lifestyle intervention, led to significant reductions in percent change in BMI compared with placebo at 72 weeks. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06075667.

title: Orforglipron for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Results From 2 Randomized Clinical Trials (ATTAIN-OSA)
abstract: IMPORTANCE: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common disorder characterized by repeated upper airway collapse during sleep that is associated with reduced quality of life and increased incidence of cardiometabolic disease. OBJECTIVE: To assess the effects of orforglipron on moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity or overweight, compared with placebo. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Two 52-week, phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials were conducted at 66 sites in the US, Argentina, Brazil, China, Czech Republic, Germany, Japan, Mexico, and Taiwan. Adults with moderate to severe OSA and body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 27 or higher were enrolled between November 11, 2024, and July 23, 2025. Final follow-up occurred on July 30, 2026. Trial 1 included patients not receiving positive airway pressure treatment and trial 2 included patients receiving positive airway pressure treatment. INTERVENTION: Patients were randomized (1:1) to receive either once-daily orforglipron (maximum tolerated dose: equivalent to 9-, 14.5-, or 17.2-mg tablet dose) or placebo. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary end point was change in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, events/h) from baseline to week 52. Seven key multiplicity-controlled secondary end points included change in sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Short Form Sleep-Related Impairment T-score, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. RESULTS: A total of 363 patients were randomized in trial 1 (mean age, 48.4 years; BMI, 37.4; AHI, 50.7 events/h; 31.4% female) and 349 patients were randomized in trial 2 (mean age, 51.1 years; BMI, 38.6; AHI, 57.6 events/h; 26.9% female). For the treatment regimen estimand, in trial 1, the mean AHI change was -17.8 for orforglipron compared with -4.5 for placebo (difference, -13.2 [95% CI, -17.7 to -8.7]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. In trial 2, the mean AHI change was -17.3 for orforglipron and -5.3 for placebo (difference, -12.0 [95% CI, -17.1 to -6.9]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. Of 7 key secondary end points, 6 were statistically significant, favoring orforglipron. Gastrointestinal events were the most commonly reported adverse events, occurring in 123 (68.0%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 68 (37.4%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 1 and in 125 (70.6%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 63 (36.6%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 2. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: These results provide evidence for the potential use of oral orforglipron to improve sleep-disordered breathing in adults with moderate to severe OSA and obesity or overweight. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06649045.

title: Trevogrumab (anti-GDF8) with or without garetosmab (anti-activin A) for prevention of muscle loss during semaglutide-induced weight reduction in people with obesity (COURAGE): a two-part, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rapid weight loss, as induced by GLP-1 receptor agonists, is accompanied by pronounced muscle loss. GDF8 (myostatin) and activin A (ActA), acting via ActRIIA/B receptors, are negative regulators of muscle mass. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of antibodies blocking GDF8 (trevogrumab) and ActA (garetosmab) on semaglutide-induced weight and muscle loss. METHODS: COURAGE is a two-part, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial. This multicentre (60 sites), US-based trial enrolled participants aged 18-80 years with obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2). In part A, participants were treated for 26 weeks with semaglutide (titrated to 2·4 mg subcutaneously weekly) in addition to a randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) concomitant treatment: placebo, trevogrumab 200 mg, trevogrumab 400 mg, or trevogrumab 400 mg and garetosmab 10 mg/kg. Trevogrumab was administered subcutaneously weekly and garetosmab was administered intravenously every 4 weeks. Part A also included a subsequent semaglutide withdrawal period, at which point participants (randomly assigned at baseline 1:1 within each group) received either trevogrumab 400 mg or placebo for an additional 26 weeks. In part B, participants were treated with semaglutide for 52 weeks and randomly assigned (1:2:2) to concomitant treatment with placebo, trevogrumab 25 mg, or trevogrumab 75 mg. Groups were stratified according to sex, BMI (<35 kg/m2vs ≥35 kg/m2), and participation in an exploratory MRI substudy assessing thigh muscle volume. Study participants, the principal investigators, and study site personnel were masked to all randomisation assignments throughout the study. Primary endpoints were percent change in lean mass, fat mass, and bodyweight from baseline to week 26 (part A) or week 52 (part B). Efficacy and safety analyses were done in all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of a study drug (efficacy, as randomly assigned; safety, as treated). COURAGE is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06299098, and is currently active, not recruiting. FINDINGS: 975 participants were enrolled between June 21, 2024, and April 14, 2025. Mean age was 49·0 years (SD 13·2) and mean BMI was 36·7 kg/m2 (SD 5·0); 627 (64%) of 975 participants were female and 348 (36%) were male. In part A (n=605, of whom n=599 received at least one dose of study drug), a substantial decrease in lean mass was observed in the semaglutide plus placebo group at week 26 (-6·6% [95% CI -7·4 to -5·7]); the estimated treatment difference (ETD) versus semaglutide plus placebo was +3·1% (95% CI 1·9 to 4·3) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 200 mg, +2·7% (1·5 to 4·0) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg, and +4·5% (3·1 to 5·9) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg. In part B (n=376), lean mass percent change from baseline to week 52 for semaglutide plus placebo was -7·3% (-8·8 to -5·8); the ETD versus semaglutide plus placebo was +1·5% (-0·3 to 3·3) for semaglutide plus trevogrumab 25 mg, and +3·1% (1·3 to 4·9) for semaglutide plus trevogrumab 75 mg. Change from baseline in fat mass in part A was -15·6% (-17·4 to -13·9) in the semaglutide plus placebo group; the ETD was significant in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg group (-3·4% [-5·9 to -0·9]) and the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (-11·7% [-14·4 to -9·0]) in part A. No other groups in part A nor any in part B had significantly different changes in fat mass compared with semaglutide plus placebo. Percent change in bodyweight in part A was -10·6 (-11·6 to -9·7) in the semaglutide plus placebo group; the ETD was significant for the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (-2·7 [-4·1 to -1·2]). No other groups in part A nor any in part B had significantly different changes in bodyweight compared with semaglutide plus placebo. Semaglutide plus trevogrumab (25 mg, 75 mg, 200 mg, or 400 mg) was generally well tolerated with a safety profile similar to semaglutide plus placebo; however, semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg had a high incidence of serious adverse events (14 [9%] of 149) and treatment discontinuations (48 [32%] of 149). Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most commonly reported, and they occurred with similar incidence across treatment groups. Muscle spasms occurred more frequently in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (61 [41%] of 149) compared with the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 200 mg or 400 mg groups (23 [8%] of 299) and semaglutide plus placebo groups (seven [5%] of 151). Most adverse events were mild to moderate in severity. Two deaths occurred during the study, both in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group; a causal association between treatment and these events was not identified. INTERPRETATION: This study establishes proof of concept for GDF8 inhibition by trevogrumab alone as a generally well tolerated strategy to preserve lean mass during GLP-1 receptor agonist-induced weight loss. Although the addition of ActA inhibition by garetosmab further improved body composition and weight loss, the combination did not have favourable safety and tolerability. Further study is required to understand whether improved body composition during weight loss might preserve physical function and overall metabolic health. FUNDING: Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

title: Efficacy and safety of efinopegdutide in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and stage 2-3 fibrosis: a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Efinopegdutide is a pharmacologically distinct once-weekly GLP-1-glucagon receptor co-agonist with a relative receptor potency balance of approximately 2:1 under development for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). We aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of efinopegdutide in adults with non-cirrhotic MASH. METHODS: We did a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind study conducted at 176 academic and community centres in 26 countries. We included adults (aged ≥18 years) with biopsy-confirmed MASH and stage 2 or stage 3 fibrosis. Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1:1) to receive either efinopegdutide (4 mg, 7 mg, or 10 mg), placebo, or open-label semaglutide 2·4 mg, all administered subcutaneously once weekly. Randomisation was performed centrally. The primary endpoint was MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis at week 52. The key secondary histological endpoint was fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis. Missing end-of-treatment biopsies were considered as failure for the primary analysis. This study is registered with EU CT, 2022-502647-35-00, and ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05877547, and is complete. FINDINGS: Between June 23, 2023, and Dec 29, 2025, we screened 1704 participants. We randomly assigned 386 (23%) participants, of whom 381 (99%; 194 [51%] women and 187 [49%] men) received at least one dose of study intervention and were included in the analysis. Baseline characteristics were similar across groups; 239 (63%) of 381 participants had F2 fibrosis and 142 (37%) had F3 fibrosis; the mean age of participants was 53 years (SD 13). At week 52, MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 31 (56%) of 55 participants in the 4 mg efinopegdutide group, 31 (63%) of 49 participants in the 7 mg efinopegdutide group, and 35 (61%) of 57 participants in the 10 mg efinopegdutide group versus seven (13%) of 53 participants in the placebo group (difference vs placebo 43·0 percentage points [95% CI 25·7 to 57·8; p<0·0001] for 4 mg, 49·5 percentage points [31·4 to 64·2; p<0·0001] for 7 mg, and 47·8 percentage points [30·7 to 62·0; p<0·0001] for 10 mg); 26 (53%) of 49 participants receiving semaglutide met this endpoint. For the key secondary endpoint, fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis occurred in 32 (43%) of 75 participants in the efinopegdutide 4 mg group, 39 (52%) of 75 participants in the 7 mg efinopegdutide group, and 26 (34%) of 77 participants in the efinopegdutide 10 mg group versus 16 (21%) of 77 participants receiving placebo (difference vs placebo 21·7 percentage points [7·1 to 35·7; p=0·0038] in the efinopegdutide 4 mg group, 30·4 percentage points [15·4 to 44·3; p<0·0001] in the efinopegdutide 7 mg group, and 13·0 percentage points [-1·2 to 26·8; p=0·072] in the efinopegdutide 10 mg group); 16 (25%) of 65 participants receiving semaglutide met this endpoint. The most frequently reported adverse events with efinopegdutide were gastrointestinal, with the highest rates among participants receiving efinopegdutide 10 mg. Adverse events leading to discontinuation of study intervention occurred more frequently among participants receiving efinopegdutide 10 mg (nine [11%] of 79 participants) compared with the other doses of efinopegdutide (range 3-4%) or placebo (one [1%]). INTERPRETATION: Treatment with efinopegdutide resulted in a significantly greater proportion of participants with MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis compared with placebo. The 7 mg dose showed the most favourable benefit-risk profile, improving fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening steatohepatitis in approximately half of participants after 1 year of treatment. These findings support the potential utility of efinopegdutide as a once-weekly GLP-1-glucagon receptor co-agonist in MASH. FUNDING: Merck Sharp & Dohme, a subsidiary of Merck & Co.

title: Cardiovascular risk, evaluation and management in patients with hypertriglyceridaemia: a Consensus Statement from the International Atherosclerosis Society
abstract: The prevalence of hypertriglyceridaemia is increasing globally owing to high rates of obesity and diabetes mellitus. Hypertriglyceridaemia is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, mediated through the cholesterol content of triglyceride-rich lipoprotein remnant particles rather than through triglycerides per se. Although plasma levels of triglycerides can be measured with a simple blood test, hypertriglyceridaemia remains underdiagnosed and undertreated. Hypertriglyceridaemia can result from various primary or secondary aetiologies, the identification and management of which is an important first step. Hypertriglyceridaemia can be managed with lifestyle measures, lipid-lowering therapy with statins in indicated patients to reduce cholesterol levels and, in refractory situations, with the addition of triglyceride-specific pharmacological therapies. Emerging therapies with considerable promise for the management of hypertriglyceridaemia include those targeting apolipoprotein C-III, angiopoietin-related protein 3 or fibroblast growth factor 21. However, so far, there is no evidence from randomized clinical trials that pharmacotherapies targeting triglycerides can reduce the occurrence of cardiovascular events, suggesting that elevated levels of triglycerides serve as a marker of atherosclerotic risk that should prompt optimization of modifiable cardiovascular risk factors. In this Consensus Statement, we provide clinical context and evidence for the evaluation, diagnosis and management of hypertriglyceridaemia.

title: ANGPTL4 Inhibition in Adults with Elevated Triglyceride Levels
abstract: BACKGROUND: Angiopoietin-like protein 4 (ANGPTL4) inhibits lipoprotein lipase and regulates triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism. MAR001 is a monoclonal antibody against ANGPTL4 that is being evaluated for lowering triglyceride levels. METHODS: We conducted a two-part, phase 2b, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. In part A, the focus of this report, we enrolled adults who had a nonfasting triglyceride level of at least 175 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 35 mg per deciliter at initial screening, followed by a fasting triglyceride level of at least 150 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 30 mg per deciliter on confirmatory screening. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to receive MAR001 at a dose of 300, 450, or 900 mg or matching placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 24 weeks. The primary end point was the percent change from baseline in the fasting triglyceride level at week 12, reported as the difference between each MAR001 dose group and the placebo group (placebo-adjusted change). RESULTS: A total of 236 participants were enrolled in the trial, with 177 assigned to receive MAR001 and 59 to receive placebo; a total of 235 participants received at least one dose of MAR001 or placebo and were included in the primary efficacy analyses. The mean age of the participants was 60.4 years, and 39% were women. The median triglyceride level at baseline was 249.5 mg per deciliter (interquartile range, 210.0 to 313.0). At week 12, in an intention-to-treat analysis, the placebo-adjusted least-squares mean percent changes in the fasting triglyceride level were -39.1 percentage points, -40.5 percentage points, and -45.3 percentage points for the 300-mg, 450-mg, and 900-mg doses, respectively (P<0.001 for all comparisons). Adverse events occurred in 123 of 177 participants (69%) in the pooled MAR001 group and in 45 of 58 participants (78%) in the placebo group. CONCLUSIONS: Inhibition of ANGPTL4 with MAR001 significantly reduced fasting triglyceride levels at 12 weeks. (Funded by Marea Therapeutics; TYDAL-TIMI 78 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT07028749.).

title: Impact of the 2026 Dyslipidemia Guideline on ASCVD Reclassification and Statin Recommendations in MESA
abstract: BACKGROUND: The 2026 American College of Cardiology (ACC)/American Heart Association (AHA)/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia recommends the use of the PREVENT (Predicting Risk of cardiovascular disease EVENTs) equations to predict atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk while concurrently revising previous risk-category thresholds. The impact of these reclassifications is yet to be described. OBJECTIVES: The authors characterized ASCVD reclassification and statin recommendations under the 2026 guideline, evaluated clinical events under this reclassification, and examined risk enhancement with risk enhancers and coronary artery calcium (CAC) burden. METHODS: Adults (N = 6,098) from the MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) were assessed, comparing the Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) and 2013 thresholds to PREVENT with 2026 thresholds. We evaluated the degree of directional reclassification, impact on statin recommendations, and risk enhancement with biomarkers and CAC burden. RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 10 years, 6.0% of participants had an ASCVD event. PREVENT reclassified 16.4% to a lower and 13.1% to a higher risk category as compared to the PCE. The statin recommendation under PREVENT was 50.4% compared to 55.2% under PCE. Of those who were no longer recommended for statin use, 4.9% went on to have an event. Individuals who were reclassified downward but had elevated CAC or any risk-enhancing factors had a higher event rate. CONCLUSIONS: Adherence to the 2026 guideline may lead to a small net downward reclassification of predicted ASCVD risk. Statin recommendations will fall modestly, however, not accompanied by a substantial number of subsequent events. Risk enhancers and elevated CAC identify higher risk subgroups than their PREVENT risk would suggest, emphasizing their supporting role in risk prediction.

title: Population Impact of the 2026 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Dyslipidemia Guideline on Lipid-Lowering Therapy Eligibility Among US Adults
abstract: BACKGROUND: The 2026 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association dyslipidemia guideline replaces the pooled cohort equations with the atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease component of the Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events equations for primary prevention risk estimation and modifies lipid-lowering therapy (LLT) eligibility by lowering the risk-based treatment threshold and expanding diabetes and chronic kidney disease criteria. The population-level impact of this transition is uncertain. METHODS: We analyzed National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2021 to 2023 participants aged 40 to 75 years without self-reported atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and with available low-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Survey weights were used to generate national estimates. Guideline-supported LLT eligibility was assessed under the 2018 pooled cohort equations-based American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association cholesterol framework and the 2026 Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events-based American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association dyslipidemia framework. Current LLT use was assessed among guideline-supported adults. RESULTS: The analytic sample included 1662 participants, representing 115.05 million US adults. LLT was supported for 42.82 million adults under the 2018 framework and 42.17 million under the 2026 framework, a net decrease of 0.65 million. Reclassification was substantial: 37.42 million remained supported, 5.40 million lost support, 4.75 million newly gained support, and 67.48 million remained unsupported. Among supported adults, current LLT use was 39.4% under the 2018 framework and 40.5% under the 2026 framework. CONCLUSIONS: Transition to the 2026 Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events-based framework produced little net change in LLT eligibility but meaningfully changed who was supported for therapy. Persistent undertreatment remains a major implementation gap.

title: Temporal Changes in Lipoprotein(a) Following Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: AIMS: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined cardiovascular risk factor generally considered stable over an individual's lifetime. Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) may transiently alter Lp(a) concentrations, complicating interpretation. We systematically evaluated temporal changes in Lp(a) following ACS. METHODS: This PRISMA 2020-guided systematic review searched MEDLINE and Embase from database inception to February 2026. Eligible studies reported serial Lp(a) measurements at two or more time points after index ACS event. Exploratory random-effects meta-analysis of percent change in mean Lp(a) was performed. RESULTS: Of 3,811 records, 16 studies comprising 1,396 patients met inclusion criteria. Lp(a) demonstrated a dynamic post-ACS trajectory. Using initial post-ACS measurements as the reference, pooled percent change in mean Lp(a) was non-significant at 24 hours post-ACS (+2.5%, 95% CI -6.8 to 11.7; p=0.602). Lp(a) was significantly higher at 7-14 days (+44.0%, 95% CI 4.0-84.1; p=0.031), 1 month (+28.3%, 95% CI 2.7-54.0; p=0.030), and 3-6 months (+22.2%, 95% CI 2.4-42.0; p=0.028). Across two studies, absolute Lp(a) increases >25 nmol/L occurred in 17% and 22% of patients by 3 and 6 months, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Lp(a) is not static post-ACS. Early post-ACS measurements may underestimate long-term concentrations and risk. Repeat measurement weeks to months later is most informative when initial post-ACS Lp(a) values are near clinical decision thresholds or would influence eligibility for emerging Lp(a)-lowering therapies.

title: Off-Pump versus On-Pump Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting in Prefrail and Frail Patients: 30-Day and 1-Year Outcomes From the FRAGILE Randomized Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Frailty is associated with worse outcomes after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). However, the comparative effectiveness of off-pump CABG (OPCAB) versus on-pump CABG (ONCAB) in prefrail and frail patients remains uncertain. METHODS: This multicenter, randomized, open-label trial enrolled patients ≥60 years of age classified as prefrail or frail, randomized 1:1, between January 2018 and December 2024. The primary outcome was a 30-day composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, or reoperation for bleeding. Secondary outcomes included ventilation time, intensive care unit and hospital stay, transfusion requirements, completeness of revascularization, surgical wound infection at 30 days, and neurocognitive function preoperatively and at 1 year. Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle; relative risks with 95% CIs were estimated. RESULTS: A total of 508 patients were included (OPCAB, n=258; ONCAB, n=250; median age, 68 years [interquartile range, 65.0-73]; 30.5% female). The primary composite outcome occurred in 28 patients receiving OPCAB (10.9%) and 40 patients receiving ONCAB (16.0%; relative risk, 1.47 [95% CI, 0.94-2.31]; P=0.09). Surgical wound infection was more frequent with ONCAB (20 [8.0%] versus 9 [3.5%]; P=0.04). No significant differences were observed in neurocognitive or quality of life outcomes at 1 year. Estimated 1-year survival probabilities were 96.1% and 92.8% in the OPCAB and ONCAB groups, respectively (P=0.099). CONCLUSION: In prefrail and frail patients undergoing CABG, OPCAB and ONCAB resulted in similar rates of the primary composite outcome. No significant differences between OPCAB and ONCAB were found in neurocognitive outcomes. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT02338947.

title: Acute aortic syndrome rule-out criteria: development and external validation
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Acute aortic syndrome (AAS) is a rare but catastrophic event, presenting with non-specific symptoms that mimic common conditions, and carries a mortality approaching 80% when missed. Current clinical tools, including the Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score (ADD-RS) and its refinement, the simplified AORTA score, achieve high sensitivity when combined with D-dimer but fail to identify a population at sufficiently low risk to safely avoid further testing. To address this gap, the Acute Aortic Syndrome Rule-Out Criteria (ARC) were developed and validated, a pragmatic bedside tool designed to safely exclude AAS in low-risk patients without additional testing. METHODS: A retrospective multistep derivation and validation study was conducted. The derivation cohort included patients with confirmed AAS from the International Registry of Acute Aortic Dissection (IRAD). Starting from existing scores, candidate predictors were identified from the IRAD dataset and sequentially added to achieve sensitivity ≥ 99%. External validation was performed in patients with suspected AAS across three prospective multicentre cohorts (ADvISED, PROFUNDUS, and DAShED). Diagnostic accuracy was assessed using sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: The final seven-variable ARC included age >60 years, abrupt onset pain, severe pain, hypotension/shock, neurological deficit, pulse deficit, and known aortic disease. Patients were classified as positive if any ARC variable was present and negative only if all variables were absent. In the derivation cohort, ARC achieved a sensitivity of 99.2% (95% CI 99.1-99.3). In the ADvISED/PROFUNDUS cohort (4598 patients, 10.2% AAS prevalence), sensitivity was 100% (95% CI 99.2-100) with specificity 23.7% (95% CI 22.4-25.0). In the DAShED cohort (5346 patients, 0.3% prevalence), sensitivity was 100% (95% CI 76.8-100) and specificity 36.4% (95% CI 35.1-37.7), ruling out 36.3% of patients without missing any AAS cases. CONCLUSIONS: ARC is an externally validated, pragmatic clinical rule demonstrating high diagnostic sensitivity in a large external validation cohort. When incorporated into existing diagnostic pathways, ARC has the potential to reduce unnecessary testing while maintaining diagnostic performance. Further prospective validation is required to confirm its clinical utility.

title: Practical Management of Multivessel Coronary Artery Disease: Evidence, Controversies, and the Boundaries of Guidelines
abstract: Multivessel coronary artery disease remains one of the most challenging cardiovascular diseases to manage. Selecting the optimal revascularization strategy requires multidisciplinary Heart Team discussion that incorporates coronary anatomy, clinical risk factors, and patient preferences into the decision-making process. Clinical guidelines provide a valuable framework for standardized, evidence-based care with reduced practice variability. However, many landmark trials enrolled highly selected populations and were conducted before the widespread adoption of contemporary revascularization techniques, including physiologic lesion assessment, intracoronary imaging, and modern arterial grafting strategies. Reflecting a collaborative Heart Team perspective, this state-of-the-art review from the American College of Cardiology Interventional Section Leadership Council and Cardiac Surgery Leadership Council summarizes contemporary evidence, reviews areas of ongoing controversy, and provides practical guidance for managing patients with multivessel coronary artery disease in clinical situations that extend beyond the scope of current guideline recommendations.

title: Nonculprit Lesion Complexity and Timing of Complete Revascularization in Patients Presenting With Acute Coronary Syndrome and Multivessel Disease: Insights From the BIOVASC Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: The optimal timing of complete revascularization for patients with acute coronary syndrome, multivessel disease and complex nonculprit coronary lesions (NCL) remains unclear. METHODS: The BIOVASC trial randomized patients with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease to immediate complete revascularization and staged complete revascularization. The primary end point was a composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, unplanned ischemia-driven revascularization, or cerebrovascular events at 2-year follow-up. In this exploratory post hoc analysis, patients were classified as having complex NCL if at least 1 nonculprit lesion met the following criteria: true bifurcation; severe calcification; lesion length >20 mm; aorto-ostial lesion; left main lesion. We aimed to compare a strategy of immediate complete revascularization and staged complete revascularization in patients presenting with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease with complex NCL. Moreover, we sought to compare patients with complex and noncomplex NCLs in terms of clinical outcomes. RESULTS: Among the 1525 patients enrolled in the BIOVASC trial, 550 (36.1%) had a complex NCL. The presence of a complex NCL was associated with a significantly higher incidence of the primary end point compared with noncomplex NCL (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.49 [95% CI, 1.11-2.02]; P=0.01), including spontaneous myocardial infarction (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.86 [95% CI, 1.12-3.09]; P=0.02). In patients with complex NCL, the cumulative incidence of the primary end point was 15.7% in the immediate complete revascularization group and 17.5% in the staged complete revascularization group (hazard ratio, 0.86 [95% CI, 0.57-1.31]; P=0.49). No significant interaction was observed between the presence of a complex NCL and revascularization strategy for the primary end point (P for interaction=0.40). CONCLUSIONS: In patients with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease, patients with complex NCL experienced worse clinical outcomes at 2-year follow-up, driven by higher rates of myocardial infarction. However, no statistically significant interaction was observed between NCL complexity and the effect of immediate complete revascularization versus staged complete revascularization. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT03621501.

title: Machine Learning Reveals Prognostic Value of Medical History in Suspected Coronary Artery Disease
abstract: BACKGROUND: Risk stratification in suspected coronary artery disease (CAD) relies on clinical history and imaging, but longitudinal medical history may provide additional prognostic information. OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated whether machine learning models using 10-year historical registry data improves prediction of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) beyond demographics and stress perfusion cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) in patients with suspected CAD. METHODS: A total of 2,159 patients (65 ± 12 years, 44% women) undergoing stress perfusion CMR were included. Models used demographics, CMR findings, and registry diagnoses and procedures from the prior 10 years. MACE was defined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or coronary intervention. Random Forest models were used for binary prediction, and Random Survival Forests (RSF) and penalized Ridge Cox regression for time-to-event analysis. RESULTS: During 2.7 ± 0.9 years of follow-up, 212 patients (9.8%) experienced MACE. For binary prediction, the area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.66 (95% CI: 0.62-0.69) using demographics and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.68-0.75; P = 0.001) after adding historical registry data. The full model achieved an AUROC of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.79-0.85) and outperformed the demographics-plus-CMR model (AUROC: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.78-0.84; ΔAUROC: 0.014; 95% CI: 0.002-0.027; P = 0.029). In time-to-event analysis, RSF and Cox regression performed similarly using demographics and CMR (concordance index [C-index] 0.80 for both; P = 0.546). After including registry data RSF achieved a C-index of 0.81 (P = 0.144), and Cox performance decreased to C-index 0.77 (P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In patients with suspected CAD, machine learning models using 10-year historical registry data have the potential to improve prognostic risk prediction beyond demographics and stress perfusion CMR.

title: Anemia and Iron Deficiency Across Renal Function in Hospitalized Heart Failure: Insights From OPPORTUNITIES Registry
abstract: BACKGROUND: Anemia and iron deficiency (ID) are highly prevalent among patients hospitalized for heart failure (HHF). Their prognostic contributions in the acute setting, particularly across kidney function, remain incompletely understood. OBJECTIVES: We investigated the association of anemia, transferrin saturation (TSAT), and ID according to kidney function, with postdischarge outcomes in HHF patients. METHODS: Consecutive HHF patients enrolled in the OPPORTUNITIES registry with available hemoglobin and TSAT at discharge. The primary endpoint was HF-free survival, a composite of all-cause death, urgent heart transplantation, heart failure (HF) hospitalization, and urgent emergency department referral for HF worsening at 12 months. Adjusted Cox regression models were applied. RESULTS: A total of 454 HHF patients were included. The median age was 77 (69-83); 37.9% were women, and 55% of patients were anemic. Anemic patients were older and exhibited a greater burden of comorbidities. Hemoglobin and TSAT showed a modest positive correlation overall (rho = 0.276, P < 0.001), which disappeared in patients with estimated glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min/1.73 m2. Lower hemoglobin was independently associated with a higher risk (adjusted HR: 0.82; 95% CI: 0.75-0.91; P < 0.001), whereas TSAT was not independently predictive. A significant interaction between hemoglobin and renal function was observed (P = 0.025), indicating that the hemoglobin effect varied according to kidney function. Among ID definitions, only TSAT <20% independently identified patients at an increased risk (HR: 1.44; 95% CI: 1.03-2.03; P = 0.035). CONCLUSIONS: In HHF patients, the prognostic relevance of anemia varies according to renal function. TSAT <20% was the only ID definition independently associated with adverse outcomes.

title: Safety and Efficacy of Omecamtiv Mecarbil by QRS Duration and Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy in GALACTIC-HF
abstract: BACKGROUND: Prolonged QRS duration portends worse outcomes in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). In GALACTIC-HF, omecamtiv mecarbil (OM) reduced the primary composite endpoint of first heart failure (HF) event or cardiovascular death. OBJECTIVES: The objectives of this study were to evaluate whether QRS duration and the presence of cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) modify the treatment effect of OM. METHODS: GALACTIC-HF enrolled patients with symptomatic HF, HFrEF (≤35%), and elevated natriuretic peptides. Baseline QRS duration was available in 8,089 of 8,232 participants (98.0%), who were classified into 3 groups: QRS duration <120 ms without CRT (n = 3,724), QRS duration ≥120 ms without CRT (n = 3,225), and CRT regardless of QRS duration (n = 1,140). The authors assessed whether the effect of OM on the primary composite endpoint, first HF hospitalization, cardiovascular death, and all-cause death differed across these groups. RESULTS: Patients with QRS ≥120 ms without CRT and those with CRT were older, had lower EF, worse health status, and higher N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels than those with QRS <120 ms without CRT. When modeled as a continuous variable, baseline QRS duration was associated with clinical outcomes among patients without CRT but not among those with CRT. Among patients with QRS ≥120 ms without CRT, OM appeared to confer less benefit for the primary composite endpoint (Pinteraction = 0.072), for cardiovascular death (Pinteraction = 0.003), and for all-cause death (Pinteraction = 0.009). In contrast, among patients treated with CRT, OM was beneficial regardless of QRS duration. CONCLUSIONS: In GALACTIC-HF, OM appeared less effective in patients with prolonged QRS duration who did not have CRT, whereas it remained beneficial in CRT-treated patients. (Global Approach to Lowering Adverse Cardiac Outcomes Through Improving Contractility in Heart Failure [GALACTIC-HF]; NCT02929329).

title: Sacubitril/valsartan for radiation-induced heart disease in children: preclinical and clinical findings
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Radiation-induced heart disease (RIHD) is a life-threatening sequela for cancer survivors. A proactive preventive strategy is urgently needed but remains elusive, particularly for the vulnerable paediatric population where prospective data are scarce. To address this gap, this study aimed to evaluate the prophylactic efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan against RIHD in children through a comprehensive translational research pipeline. METHODS: A prospective observational study was first conducted in 40 paediatric solid tumour patients, comparing cardiac function before and 1 week after radiotherapy, with 80 healthy controls. A juvenile rat RIHD model was then established, in which the efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan was assessed and validated through longitudinal echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, histopathology, bulk RNA-seq, and single-nucleus RNA-seq. Finally, a prospective clinical cohort (n = 15 sacubitril/valsartan, n = 15 control) was conducted in paediatric patients post-radiotherapy, with a 12-month follow-up for efficacy and safety. RESULTS: In paediatric patients, radiotherapy significantly impaired biventricular function, notably reducing left ventricular global longitudinal strain, and mean heart radiation dose was significantly correlated with cardiac function impairment. In juvenile rats, sacubitril/valsartan attenuated pathological ventricular wall thickening, myocardial fibrosis, diastolic dysfunction, and perfusion deficits. Mechanistically, it mitigated endothelial cell damage and immune cell activation, promoted a macrophage phenotypic shift from M1 to M2, suppressed fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition, and broadly attenuated pro-fibrotic and inflammatory cell-cell communication. In the clinical cohort, sacubitril/valsartan significantly improved left ventricular global longitudinal strain and aortic compliance vs controls, with a favourable safety profile. CONCLUSIONS: This first-in-kind translational study demonstrates that early prophylaxis with sacubitril/valsartan is a feasible and effective strategy to mitigate radiation-induced cardiotoxicity in children. These findings, underpinned by multi-modal validation from bench to bedside, challenge the reactive management paradigm in paediatric cardio-oncology and establish a foundational evidence base for a new standard of proactive heart care in childhood cancer survivors.

title: Advanced Age in Acute Myocardial Infarction-Related Cardiogenic Shock by Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Status
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiogenic shock (CS) remains a leading cause of in-hospital mortality in acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Although advanced age is associated with worse outcomes, associations across out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) strata remain incompletely characterized. OBJECTIVES: The objective of the study was to evaluate the association between octogenarian status and in-hospital mortality in patients with AMI-related CS (AMI-CS) undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and to examine this association in analyses stratified by OHCA status. METHODS: We analyzed patients with AMI-CS enrolled in the multicenter Kanagawa-ACuTe cardIoVascular rEgistry who underwent PCI. Octogenarian status (≥80 years) was the primary exposure. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate associations with in-hospital mortality, with additional analyses stratified by OHCA status. RESULTS: Among 658 patients, 177 (26.9%) were octogenarians, and 279 (42.4%) died during hospitalization. Octogenarian status was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR: 2.14; 95% CI: 1.32-3.48; P = 0.002). In stratified analyses, octogenarian status was associated with higher mortality among patients without OHCA, whereas no statistically significant association was observed among those with OHCA. The interaction between octogenarian status and OHCA was not statistically significant (P for interaction = 0.422). Higher heart rate, unmeasurable heart rate, higher serum creatinine, and lower serum albumin were independently associated with mortality. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with AMI-CS undergoing PCI, octogenarian status was independently associated with in-hospital mortality. Although estimates differed numerically across OHCA strata, the interaction was not statistically significant, precluding a conclusion that the association differed according to OHCA status. These stratified findings should therefore be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Chronological age should be considered within a comprehensive clinical assessment rather than in isolation.

title: Thirty-Day All-Cause Readmissions After Pregnancy-Associated Hospitalizations With Heart Failure in the United States: Analysis of the Nationwide Readmissions Database
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of pregnancy-related morbidity and mortality in the United States. There is a paucity of data regarding pregnancy-associated heart failure readmissions. This study aims to characterize the 30-day heart failure readmission patterns in pregnancy-associated admissions. METHODS: The National Readmission Database from 2016 to 2021 was used to identify women aged 13 to 49 with an index hospitalization with heart failure as the primary or secondary diagnosis during a pregnancy-related admission, identified by diagnosis-related group codes and International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause readmission. Survey-weighted descriptive analyses and hierarchical multivariable logistic regression were used to characterize readmission patterns and identify independently associated factors. RESULTS: Among 19 452 eligible index hospitalizations, 2659 were followed by a 30-day readmission; the survey-weighted readmission rate was 13.5%. In the fully adjusted model, Medicare and Medicaid coverage, residence in a small metropolitan area, greater All Patient Refined Diagnosis-Related Group severity, discharge with home health care, and discharge against medical advice were associated with higher odds of readmission. Deficiency anemia, chronic pulmonary disease, diabetes without chronic complications, renal failure, solid tumor without metastasis, and cardiovascular or respiratory disorders complicating pregnancy were also independently associated with increased readmission. CONCLUSIONS: Approximately 1 in 7 pregnancy-associated hospitalizations complicated by heart failure was followed by a 30-day all-cause readmission. Readmission risk reflected a combination of illness severity, discharge disposition, payer status, geographic location, and selected medical and pregnancy-related comorbidities. These findings support the development and evaluation of individualized, multidisciplinary transitional-care strategies for patients at highest risk.

title: Myocardial Responses to Eplontersen in Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy: The CARDIO-TTRansform CMR study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Transthyretin-lowering therapies target the underlying cause of transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), but their effects on myocardial amyloid burden and cardiac remodelling remain incompletely characterized. We evaluated the myocardial effects of sustained transthyretin suppression with eplontersen using serial multiparametric cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR). METHODS: This CMR study was a pre-specified, international, prospective study embedded within the randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 CARDIO-TTRansform trial. Participants underwent CMR at baseline and planned assessments at weeks 25, 49, 97, and 140. The primary imaging analysis evaluated longitudinal changes in CMR parameters using mixed models for repeated measures. Myocardial amyloid regression and progression were defined as ≥5 percentage-point decreases and increases in extracellular volume (ECV), respectively. All other patients were considered stable. RESULTS: We enrolled 120 participants with baseline and ≥1 follow-up CMR assessment (eplontersen, n=58; placebo, n=62; mean age, 76.7±6.5 years; 95% male; baseline stabilizer, 12.5%). At week 140 eplontersen resulted in lower ECV, compared with placebo (least-squares mean difference [95% CI], -6.7 percentage points [ -8.7 to -4.7]; P<0.001) and lower native T1 ( -25.9ms [-41.7 to -10.2 ]; P=0.002) and left ventricular mass (-19.1g [-28.0 to -10.2]; P<0.001). Eplontersen also increased left ventricular ejection fraction (+5.1% [1.8-8.3]; P=0.002), right ventricular ejection fraction (+4.6% [0.6-8.7]; P=0.03), and left ventricular global longitudinal, circumferential, and radial strain and right ventricular longitudinal strain (all P<0.05), compared to placebo. At week-140, myocardial amyloid regression occurred in 12.5% receiving eplontersen versus 0% receiving placebo, whereas progression occurred in 12.5% versus 76%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Sustained transthyretin suppression with eplontersen resulted in substantially lower myocardial ECV and favorable changes in cardiac structure, biventricular systolic function, and myocardial deformation compared with placebo in a cohort of patients mostly not on background stabilizer at baseline. These findings provide randomized evidence that lowering circulating transthyretin modifies myocardial disease progression in ATTR-CM and support serial multiparametric CMR for characterizing myocardial treatment response.

title: Effects of Eplontersen on Cardiac Structure and Function in Patients With Transthyretin Amyloidosis With Cardiomyopathy: Insights from the CARDIO-TTRansform Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: In CARDIO-TTRansform, the TTR (transthyretin) silencer eplontersen did not significantly reduce the primary end point of cardiovascular death and recurrent cardiovascular events in patients with TTR amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy, although treatment effects varied by baseline TTR stabilizer use. Whether eplontersen favorably affects cardiac structure and function is unknown. METHODS: CARDIO-TTRansform randomized 1432 patients with TTR amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy to eplontersen (45 mg) subcutaneously every 4 weeks or placebo. Echocardiograms were performed at baseline and weeks 61, 97, and 140. Associations of baseline echocardiographic measures with all-cause mortality and the primary end point were evaluated using Cox and semiparametric proportional rates models. Between-group differences at week 140 were analyzed with mixed models for repeated measures. RESULTS: Among 1426 participants with baseline echocardiograms (mean age, 76±7 years, 91% men, 85% wild type, 57% receiving stabilizers), baseline measures of left ventricular systolic function (LV ejection fraction, global longitudinal strain, stroke volume, myocardial contraction fraction), diastolic function (E wave deceleration time, septal e', average E/e'), and right ventricular function and hemodynamics were independently associated with all-cause mortality or the primary end point. At week 140 (echocardiograms available in 554 patients in the eplontersen group and 506 in the placebo group), eplontersen attenuated increases in mean LV wall thickness (least-squares mean [LSM] difference, -0.24 mm [95% CI, -0.48 to -0.01]) and declines in LV stroke volume (LSM difference, 1.88 mL [95% CI, 0.07-3.69]), myocardial contraction fraction (LSM difference, 0.88% [95% CI, 0.25-1.57]), average E/e' (LSM difference, -0.71 [95% CI, -1.36 to -0.07]), and right ventricular outflow tract velocity-time integral (LSM difference, 0.42 [95% CI, 0.00-0.85]) versus placebo in the overall cohort. Beneficial effects were driven almost exclusively by patients not receiving stabilizers at baseline. No significant treatment effects were observed in patients receiving stabilizers. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with TTR amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy, eplontersen modestly attenuated deterioration in prognostically important measures of LV systolic, diastolic and right ventricular function, primarily among patients not receiving stabilizers at baseline. These findings complement the clinical findings of CARDIO-TTRansform and suggest that TTR silencing may attenuate progression of cardiac dysfunction in TTR amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT04136171; URL: xxx; Unique identifier: 2019-002835-27.

title: Incremental yield of genetic retesting in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Modern genetic testing in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) includes newly described HCM-associated genes and full intronic regions of certain classic sarcomeric genes. This study evaluated genetic retesting in HCM patients with a prior negative test and identified predictors of a positive result to guide retesting. METHODS: This multicentre study included patients with HCM who previously had negative next-generation sequencing (NGS)-based genetic testing at four centres. Subjects were retested using an updated NGS-based HCM panel. RESULTS: Of 508 retested HCM patients (median age 70 years; 66.9% male; median maximal left ventricular wall thickness 18 mm; median interval from initial genetic test 6.6 years), 46 (9%) had 48 HCM-related variants: 14 in new HCM-associated genes, 3 in deep intronic MYBPC3 regions, 18 intermediate-effect variants, and 13 (8 reclassified) in classic HCM-associated genes. In multivariable analysis, the presence of late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) [odds ratio (OR) 3.52; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.38-10.25], the Mayo HCM score (OR 1.46 per 1 point increase; 95% CI 1.08-2.01), and the Toronto HCM score (OR 1.18 per 1 point increase; 95% CI 1.08-1.30) were independent predictors of detecting HCM-related variants at retesting. The diagnostic yields in patients with LGE and a high Toronto score (≥13 points), and with LGE and a high Mayo score (≥4 points), were 80% and 50%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with HCM and prior negative genetic testing, retesting identified HCM-related variants in 9% of individuals, allowing counselling and risk stratification. Late gadolinium enhancement, combined with the Mayo and Toronto scores, may be used to guide which patients should be prioritized for genetic retesting.

title: Artificial intelligence-enhanced electrocardiography for detection and prediction of dilated cardiomyopathy
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: A major challenge in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) care is the identification and management of individuals at risk before disease manifestation. An artificial intelligence (AI) model applied to electrocardiography (ECG) was developed to detect and predict the echocardiographic DCM phenotype (left ventricular dilatation with systolic dysfunction) and was evaluated for its ability to stratify the risk of incident DCM in familial cohorts. METHODS: A deep learning model was trained to detect the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and to predict its future onset, using more than 330 000 ECG-echocardiogram pairs from the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston. Model performance was validated in cohorts from the UK Biobank, Zhongshan Hospital, and Antwerp University Hospital, and compared with models based on traditional ECG features and echocardiographic traits. To assess performance in familial DCM, genetically predisposed individuals identified through cascade screening at the cardiogenetics clinics of Antwerp University Hospital (n = 166, 18% DCM positive) and Maastricht University Medical Center (n = 177, 18% DCM positive) were evaluated. RESULTS: The AI-ECG model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of .87-.97 for diagnosing the prevalent DCM phenotype, outperforming traditional ECG parameters. AI-ECG was comparable to echocardiography for predicting future DCM (C-index .80-.87 and .80-.90, respectively). In familial cohorts, 5-year negative predictive values were 95.5% (Antwerp) and 91.5% (Maastricht), with corresponding positive predictive values of 42.4% and 39.4%, while high-risk scores were associated with a 5.1-6.4-fold increased risk of incident DCM. CONCLUSIONS: The explainable AI-ECG model detects the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and predicts future disease, and supports the exclusion of short- to mid-term disease in genetically at-risk individuals. This low-cost tool could help reduce surveillance burden and facilitate earlier intervention.

title: Risk Stratification and Outcomes of Right Atrial Phasic Function in Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy: A Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Advanced arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is associated with a high risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmias (MVA) and end-stage heart failure (HF). However, the prognostic role of right atrial (RA) mechanics, as quantified by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR), remains largely unexplored. METHODS: Consecutive patients with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy undergoing CMR between 2014 and 2021 were retrospectively included. Demographics, clinical history, and strain parameters were collected. The primary clinical end points were end-stage HF and MVA. RESULTS: A total of 316 patients (mean age 38±15 years; 66.1% men) were included. Over a median follow-up of 5.3 years, 49 developed end-stage HF and 103 experienced MVA outcomes. Multivariable Cox and Fine-Gray models showed that impaired RA reservoir strain was an independent predictor of end-stage HF (hazard ratio [HR] 0.92, 95% CI 0.89-0.96, P<0.001) and MVA outcomes (subdistribution hazard ratio (sHR) 0.98, 95% CI 0.96-0.99, P=0.025), with added prognostic value beyond clinical and imaging variables, improving the C-statistic to 0.84 and 0.70, respectively. Kaplan-Meier survival curves indicated that RA reservoir strain <18.6% was associated with higher end-stage HF risk, consistent across subgroups regardless of left ventricular involvement (both log-rank P<0.05). The association between RA reservoir strain <23.0% and MVA was significant in the overall cohort (P<0.001) and in patients without left ventricular involvement (P=0.002), but not in those with left ventricular involvement (P=0.08). CONCLUSIONS: Lower cardiac magnetic resonance-derived RA reservoir strain was independently associated with end-stage HF and MVA in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and provided incremental prognostic value beyond conventional risk markers. These findings support RA mechanics as a potential complementary component of multichamber CMR risk assessment, pending external validation.

title: Prevalence and Consequences of Guideline-Directed Indications for Aortic Valve Replacement in the EARLY TAVR Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: The current American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association valvular heart disease guidelines were published before several recent trials that provide greater support for early intervention in patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis (AS). OBJECTIVES: This study sought to investigate the prevalence and clinical impact of American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Class II recommendations for AVR in the EARLY TAVR trial. METHODS: The EARLY TAVR trial randomized patients with asymptomatic severe AS to transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance (CS) with conversion to TAVR based on development of ACC/AHA Class I indications. Patients in the intention-to-treat cohort were stratified by presence of a Class II indication for AVR at randomization. The primary endpoint of the present analysis was the composite of all-cause death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization. Interaction tests were performed to assess whether the treatment effect differed by level of guideline recommendation. Timing of conversion to AVR in the CS group according to the presence/absence of Class II indications was also assessed. RESULTS: Of the 901 patients randomized to TAVR (N = 445) and CS (N = 446), 636 (70.6%) patients had no guideline recommendation, and 265 (29.4%) had at least1 1 Class II recommendation for AVR at the time of randomization. At a median follow-up of 3.8 years, patients with a Class II indication for AVR experienced higher rates of the primary endpoint (Class II: 24.5% vs no recommendation: 14.5%; HR = 1.78; 95% CI: 1.30-2.44; P < 0.001) and were more likely to have acute valve syndrome at the time of conversion. Compared with CS, the relative benefit of early TAVR on the primary endpoint was similar regardless of the presence or absence of a Class II guideline recommendation (HR = 0.62; 95% CI: 0.37-1.02 vs 0.61; 95% CI: 0.40-0.92; Pinteraction = 0.96). CONCLUSIONS: Among patients in the EARLY TAVR trial, Class II indications for AVR were present in almost one-third of patients at baseline. The benefit of early TAVR was consistent regardless of the presence or absence of Class II indications. These findings support the strategy of early TAVR over CS in asymptomatic patients with severe AS, independent of guideline indications. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03042104; Unique Identifier: NCT03042104.

title: Transcatheter vs Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement for Isolated Native Aortic Regurgitation: National Propensity-Matched Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is well established for aortic stenosis, while its application for isolated native aortic regurgitation (AR) was previously off label and technically challenging. Comparative data between TAVR and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) are limited. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to compare patient characteristics and outcomes of off-label TAVR vs SAVR among patients with isolated native AR. METHODS: Using the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Medicare Provider Analysis and Review database, patients ≥65 years of age who underwent TAVR or SAVR for isolated native AR (2017-2023) were identified.
